relationship: Sulfur and the destruction of dwellings
rationale: Bildad joins lodging in the tent with splendid things strewn with sulfur. Genesis uses sulfur in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah; this is a comparison of destructive imagery, not an assertion that Bildad names those cities or describes the same event.

relationship: The fate of a person's memorial and name
rationale: Bildad wishes the memorial to perish but adds that the person has a name on the land's outer face. Proverbs contrasts praised righteous memory with an extinguished impious name; the shared concern with remembrance is retained without erasing that different name clause.

relationship: Job's judgments about his own speech
rationale: Job admits words that wandered untimely. Later, after hearing the Lord, he asks what answer he can give, places a hand over his mouth and resolves to add nothing further; the comparison concerns his own assessments and restraint of speech, not a confession to every accusation made against him.

relationship: Words preserved on stone
rationale: Job wishes for a record with an iron stylus and lead, or for words engraved in rocks. Deuteronomy commands the law written on plastered stones; the stone-record comparison preserves the different texts and methods rather than combining Job's alternatives into one technique.

relationship: A warning about wrath and God's rebuke of the friends
rationale: Job warns his opponents about wrath and lawlessness. God's final reproof and threatened destruction concern the friends' untrue speech; this narrative connection does not claim the target explicitly uses wrath language, and no sword is imported into Job's covering wording.

relationship: Unjust acquisition pictured as forced disgorgement
rationale: Zophar says unjust wealth is vomited out and that an angel will drag it from the person's house. Jeremiah pictures Babylon being made to disgorge what she swallowed; the shared expulsion image does not identify the owner, angel or city across passages.

relationship: Honey and dairy abundance granted or withheld
rationale: Zophar wishes that the wicked person not see milking herds or honey-and-butter pastures. Deuteronomy recounts God providing honey, cattle butter and sheep milk; the connection contrasts access to those concrete signs of abundance.

relationship: Possessions offer no secure outcome
rationale: Zophar says there is no deliverance for the person's possessions and that he will not be saved in his desire. Sirach warns that unjust possessions bring no benefit in calamity; the comparison preserves for possessions rather than rewriting it as through possessions.

relationship: The wrongdoer himself and the consequences borne by children
rationale: Job wishes that possessions fail the sons and states that the man himself will be repaid. Ezekiel expressly distinguishes the son's and father's responsibility; the connection highlights personal recompense without pretending Job's property-loss wish states the same complete legal rule.

relationship: Accused mistreatment of widows and orphans versus Job's account
rationale: Eliphaz alleges sending widows away empty and mistreating orphans. Job later recalls helping an orphan and receiving a widow's blessing; the comparison keeps accusation and self-testimony distinct.

relationship: An instruction to keep God's words and Job's reply
rationale: Eliphaz urges Job to take God's utterance and set His words in his heart. Job's next reply says he will not transgress and has already hidden the words in his breast, answering the implication that this inward obedience still needs to begin.

relationship: Prayer heard in the narrative's ending
rationale: Eliphaz promises that Job's prayer will be heard. At the end Job prays for the friends and the Lord forgives their sin; the narrative correspondence preserves the reversal that the friends themselves need his intercession.

relationship: Seeking God and the eventual encounter
rationale: Job longs to find Him and reach an end. At the close Job contrasts former hearing with his eye now seeing God; this is a narrative movement from sought encounter to encounter, without inserting a throne or seat into the present wording.

relationship: God's action escapes Job's perception
rationale: Job did not grasp God's action on the left and will not see when He wraps around the right. His earlier statement that God can pass by without being seen or perceived develops the same difficulty of access, without assigning cardinal directions to the preceding unit.

relationship: Guarding the commanded way without turning aside
rationale: Job says he will go out in God's commands, has guarded His ways and will not turn aside. The psalm connects restrained feet, keeping divine words and not departing from judgments; these are corresponding professions of obedience with their different verb forms preserved.

relationship: Darkness before Job's face
rationale: Job says he had not known darkness would come, and that gloom covered what lay before his face. His earlier complaint also placed darkness before his face; this repeated image remains a report of experienced distress rather than a confession of hidden crimes.

relationship: Pledges taken from widows and justice for orphans
rationale: Job describes leading away the orphans' pack animal and taking a widow's cow as a pledge. Deuteronomy protects orphan and widow justice and forbids a widow's garment as pledge; the pledge is not extended to the pack animal, and cow and garment remain distinct objects.

relationship: Violence against orphans and the law's protection
rationale: Job describes an orphan snatched from the breast and the humbling of one who had fallen. Exodus prohibits mistreating orphans and warns that their cries will bring wrath; the comparison does not invent a debt-enslavement mechanism for the snatching.

relationship: Taking from orphans and the threatened consequence
rationale: Job connects plants appearing dried up with an armful snatched from orphans. Exodus warns of judgment for mistreating orphans; the connection preserves the different stated consequences and does not substitute snow or Hades for Job's wording.

relationship: Divine command over the lights of heaven
rationale: Bildad says the moon fails to shine at God's command and that stars are not pure before Him. Job earlier said God speaks to the sun and it does not rise, and seals the stars; the comparison concerns control of luminaries, with moon, sun and purity claims kept distinct.

relationship: Thunder and the limits of human understanding
rationale: Job contrasts the mere drop heard of His ways with the strength of His thunder and asks who knows when He will act. Elihu later joins divine thunder with great works not known to humans; both connect thunder with limited understanding, while remaining distinct speakers.
